claims.text: The Cr-free Hf-Mo-Ta-Ti-Zr alloy has a single-phase BCC structure.
Asymmetric XRD peaks in the Cr-free alloy are caused by dendritic versus interdendritic compositional micro-segregation.
The Cr-free alloy has anomalously low room-temperature fracture strain.
During solidification, added Cr segregates preferentially to interdendritic regions.
Approximately 4 at.% Cr destabilizes the BCC matrix and drives Laves-phase precipitation.
The Cr-induced secondary phase is specifically a C14 Laves phase.
The C14 Laves phase forms a reticulated, interconnected network in Cr-rich interdendritic zones.
The Cr-induced Laves phase occupies approximately 4 vol.% of the alloy.
Laves-phase precipitation reduces atomic-radius misfit and elastic energy in the BCC solid solution, thereby promoting decomposition.
Cr and the other differently sized solutes produce local lattice distortion that impedes dislocation motion and causes solid-solution hardening.
The reticulated Laves-phase morphology impedes crack extension by causing crack deflection and branching.
The interconnected Laves network lowers fracture strain because it is brittle.
The Cr-added alloy has significantly higher yield strength than the baseline through combined precipitation and solid-solution hardening.
Adding Cr contracts the BCC lattice parameter relative to the Cr-free baseline.
The Cr-free baseline contains no Laves-phase precipitates.
Lattice contraction beyond a critical threshold changes the Laves phase to a needle-like morphology or causes immediate catastrophic failure.
Keeping the Laves-phase fraction near 4 vol.% preserves a reticulated morphology rather than a continuous brittle network.
The Laves-phase volume fraction depends on cooling rate and the thermodynamic stability of Cr-rich interdendritic regions.

contradictions.description: The Laves network is said to impede crack extension through deflection and branching, but it is also predicted to lower fracture strain. The falsification rule further says that higher fracture strain would indicate that the phase did not impede cracks, whereas effective crack impediment would ordinarily be expected to increase resistance to fracture. The competing crack-arrest and embrittlement effects are not separated or assigned a net quantitative criterion.
